title: Introduction to Hashing
objective: Understand why hash tables provide efficient data retrieval.

sections.title: What is a hash table?
sections.content: A hash table is a data structure that stores keys in positions determined by a hash function.

sections.title: Why use hash tables?
sections.content: Hash tables can provide efficient average-case lookup by using a hash function to calculate where a key should be stored.

title: Hash Functions
objective: Calculate the home slot using key mod table size.

sections.title: The modulo hash function
sections.content: The home slot can be calculated by dividing the key by the table size and using the remainder.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: For key 23 and table size 10, the home slot is 23 mod 10 = 3.

title: Understanding Collisions
objective: Identify when two keys map to the same table position.

sections.title: What is a collision?
sections.content: A collision occurs when two different keys map to the same home slot.

title: Linear Probing
objective: Insert keys using linear probing, including wrap-around.

sections.title: Resolving collisions
sections.content: Linear probing checks the next slot until an empty position is found. When the end of the table is reached, the search wraps around to the beginning.

title: Searching in Hash Tables
objective: Trace a search and determine when an unsuccessful search stops.

sections.title: Searching
sections.content: A search begins at the key's home slot and follows the linear probing sequence until the key is found or an empty slot is reached.

title: Clustering and Load Factor
objective: Analyse how clustering and load factor affect performance.

sections.title: Clustering
sections.content: Clustering occurs when occupied slots form groups, potentially increasing the number of positions examined.

sections.title: Load factor
sections.content: Load factor is the proportion of table slots that are occupied.
